newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Doctor says Yeltsin depressed at new illness.
newsitem.headline: Doctor says Yeltsin depressed at new illness.

text.p: A doctor treating President Boris Yeltsin for pneumonia on Friday described the Russian leader as a man who pushed himself to the limit and said he was depressed at falling sick so soon after his heart operation.

Sergei Mironov, head of the Kremlin medical centre, told a news briefing at the Central Clinical Hospital that Yeltsin would remain there for at least another three days and spend another three weeks recovering at home.

Mironov said the pneumonia was not linked to Yeltsin's bypass surgery on November 5 and that there were no grounds for pessimism. But he made clear Yeltsin's morale had suffered and he had been reluctant to return to hospital.
"He should have been brought here a few days earlier and we proposed this," Mironov said.
"But it is possible to understand him purely psychologically. The man had just recovered from one very serious problem when a second one appeared, though it was a smaller one.

"I understand him as a person but as a doctor I have another position. Of course I cannot say Boris Nikolayevich feels comfortable spiritually. Of course this is depressing him, of course his mood is not a very happy one but I see no reason for particular pessimism."
Yeltsin would recover at his residence but he would not be isolated completely from visitors to protect him from a flu epidemic which has hit Moscow in recent weeks, he said.

"This illness is not something extreme. The increased media and public attention could be explained by a desire to link his illness to the surgery. I can say clearly -- there is no connection here," Mironov added.
Mironov portrayed the 65-year-old Kremlin leader as a man who was determined to do everything for himself.
After his operation Yeltsin had "not been prepared to do things by halves" but wanted to push himself to the limit. "'Must' always was his motto. He always was a man of duty," Mironov said.
But there was a sign on Friday that Yeltsin could be facing up to his limitations.
The Russian leader asked for a Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit which he was due to attend in Moscow on January 17 to be postponed.
Officials said the decision was not linked to Yeltsin's illness and blamed the postponement on organisational problems.

CIS secretary Ivan Korotchenya told Reuters in the capital of Belarus that Yeltsin had also requested the delay to allow Uzbekistan's President Islam Karimov, who had planned another foreign trip, to attend.
But it seemed likely the decision was at least partly connected to Yeltsin's recuperation, considering his anticipated three-week recovery period at home.

Looking to the future, Mironov said he did not think the pneumonia would lead to a string of illnesses but added: "We should cure the president properly and restore his condition of one week ago. This will be the best guarantee against more illnesses and difficulties."
